items.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a 816B-parameter multimodal AI model optimized for Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1M-token context window and agentic capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Muse Spark Open
items.summary:
Meta has launched Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion parameter multimodal AI model designed for complex coding, multi-step reasoning, and long-horizon tasks. The model supports a 1 million token context window and is optimized to run on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using the MLX framework, enabling powerful on-device AI workflows.

Muse Spark Open is available through multiple API platforms and cloud providers, with weights downloadable from Amazon SageMaker, Google Cloud, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It supports various inference engines and hardware optimizations, allowing developers to customize it via PyTorch. Meta has implemented safety measures and released the model under a license permitting many free commercial uses.

items.title: Researcher finds neural networks are inherently interpretable, challenging prior beliefs about polysemanticity and superposition in image and language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural networks are clean
items.summary: A researcher studying neural networks in image and language models has concluded that these networks are inherently interpretable, contradicting earlier views that networks pack concepts arbitrarily through polysemanticity and superposition. The study suggests that what appeared as complex entanglement was actually a form of recursive generalization, making mechanistic interpretability more feasible than previously thought. Improvements in network architecture have increased neuron interpretability, with modern models showing clearer, more legible structures across scales. This challenges the prior assumption that neural networks require complex unfolding or reconstruction to be understood.

items.title: Krea 3 launches a production-ready image editing model that edits only specified areas, operates at native 2K resolution, and completes edits faster and cheaper than competitors [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Krea 3 – An image model built for editing at scale
items.summary:
Krea 3 is a new image editing model designed for production use, enabling precise edits that change only user-specified parts of an image while preserving the rest. It completes edits in about 8 seconds at a cost of approximately $0.06 per image, outperforming similar models in speed and cost efficiency. The model supports up to eight reference images, matches exact colors by hex code, and maintains character consistency across edits, all rendered natively at 2K resolution.

The model is integrated into workflows for designers working on posters, branding, and covers, allowing rapid, voice-driven edits and offering 251 launch presets. Krea 3 is distributed through leading organizations and aims to streamline image editing by reducing wait times and costs while maintaining high precision and detail. The company provides support for prototyping, development, and scaling AI solutions with Krea 3.

items.title: Developer uses AI to reverse engineer hardware drivers, creating a generic harness to aid Linux support for unsupported devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Using AI to reverse engineer hardware
items.summary:
A developer applied AI tools, specifically Claude, to reverse engineer hardware drivers for devices lacking Linux support, such as a Plustek 8200i scanner and a laptop MIPI camera. By capturing USB traffic and comparing Windows driver behavior with Linux attempts, the AI helped generate working drivers and patches, significantly reducing the manual effort typically required.

The developer created a generic harness called hw-harness to automate capturing and diffing USB traffic between Windows and Linux drivers, enabling AI to identify driver bugs and propose fixes. This approach avoids copying code and instead extracts configuration data from Windows drivers, making it easier for others to apply AI-assisted reverse engineering to their own hardware challenges.

items.title: Researchers propose confidence-calibrated controller for evaluator-guided test-time reasoning that reduces compute by up to 30% while maintaining utility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Confidence-Calibrated Inference Expansion for Evaluator-Guided Test-Time Reasoning
items.summary: Researchers introduce a compute-aware three-action controller for evaluator-guided reasoning that decides whether to trust the current answer, fallback, or spend more inference based on predicted success and compute cost. The approach includes a local action-gap analysis and expected regret bounds to guide learning and calibration of confidence estimates with uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. Evaluations on width expansion and revision tasks show the controller improves utility over fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively, framing evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty rather than uniformly stronger reasoning.
items.description: Researchers introduce a compute-aware three-action controller for evaluator-guided reasoning that decides whether to trust the current answer, fallback, or spend more inference based on predicted success and compute cost. The approach includes a local action-gap analysis and expected regret bounds to guide learning and calibration of confidence estimates with uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. Evaluations on width expansion and revision tasks show the controller improves utility over fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively, framing evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty rather than uniformly stronger reasoning.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluator-guided reasoning presents a local control problem at every step: trust the current answer, return a fallback, or spend more inference. We formulate this choice as a compute-aware three-action controller, scoring terminal actions by predicted answer success and expansion by a rollout-based continuation-success surrogate, with compute cost priced explicitly. A local action-gap analysis characterizes when score errors can change a decision, while an expected regret bound accounts for errors along the realized expansion path. Guided by this analysis, we learn and calibrate action-specific confidence estimates, with local uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. On held-out width expansion and revision tasks, the controller improves observed utility over calibration-selected fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively. Across four Qwen3-8B seeds, compute is lower than fitted Q in both settings, while utility differences are small and mixed. The results frame evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty, rather than a uniformly stronger reasoner.

items.title: Researchers present LEV, a looped decision model that improves accuracy by rerunning layers for deeper reasoning without generating tokens, achieving up to 76.2% accuracy on JevBench [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LEV: Thinking Fast and Deep with Looped Decision Models
items.summary:
Researchers introduce LEV, a decision model that enhances reasoning depth by looping through its layers multiple times instead of generating text tokens. LEV is built on a language model pretrained as a loop and can adjust its reasoning depth per question, improving accuracy especially on harder problems. Experiments show that a 2.6 billion parameter LEV model increases accuracy from 63.2% at one loop to 76.2% at four loops on the JevBench dataset, while saving computation with an on-demand stopping mechanism.

The model's design allows a single checkpoint to operate at various depths, trained jointly across all steps. On locked test sets, LEV models with 1.4 billion and 3 billion parameters outperform comparable non-looped models by 5.4 to 8.8 accuracy points while maintaining latency under 50 milliseconds. This approach offers a flexible trade-off between computational cost and accuracy, particularly benefiting difficult decision tasks.
items.description:

LEV is built on a language model pretrained as a loop and can adjust its reasoning depth per question, improving accuracy especially on harder problems. Experiments show that a 2.6 billion parameter LEV model increases accuracy from 63.2% at one loop to 76.2% at four loops on the JevBench dataset, while saving computation with an on-demand stopping mechanism.

The model's design allows a single checkpoint to operate at various depths, trained jointly across all steps. On locked test sets, LEV models with 1.4 billion and 3 billion parameters outperform comparable non-looped models by 5.4 to 8.8 accuracy points while maintaining latency under 50 milliseconds. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Decision models answer typed questions about an input with one probability per option, computed in a single forward pass without generating text. Like the fast System 1 of dual-process theory, they answer at once, but their depth is fixed at training time, so they spend the same computation on easy and hard questions. Models that reason in generated text can think longer, but they pay for every extra step in decoded tokens. We present LEV, a decision model that thinks deeper by rerunning its layers in a loop instead of generating tokens. LEV builds on a language model pretrained as a loop, reads the options after every loop step and trains all steps jointly, so one checkpoint can answer at any depth. On three looped backbones, accuracy rises with depth on the same weights, mostly on hard questions, and a 2.6B LEV goes from 63.2% at depth one to 76.2% at depth four on JevBench. On-demand depth, set per question by a small stopper with a threshold fitted on unlabelled requests, saves 15% to 24% of the computation at a cost of under one accuracy point, level with or slightly above a fixed mix of depths. On a locked test set, the 1.4B and 3B models are 5.4 to 8.8 points more accurate than dense (non-looped) models and cascades of the same latency below 50 ms.

items.title: Athanor system enables autonomous AI agents to post-train a base model into a generalist model matching official instruct versions in 104 hours [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Athanor: An Agent-Native System for Autonomous Post-Training Research
items.summary: Athanor is an open agent-native system designed for autonomous post-training research on GPUs, allowing AI agents full autonomy to improve base models without external guidance. In a 104-hour experiment, four Claude Opus 5.5 agents collaboratively enhanced the Qwen3-4B-Base model, achieving performance comparable to or exceeding the official instruct version on multiple evaluation suites. The agents independently managed data processing, algorithm modification, hyperparameter tuning, and result analysis within a sandboxed environment, using known methods such as supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, weight merging, and self-distillation. This demonstration marks the first time frontier agents have autonomously post-trained a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model, suggesting that current AI agents possess the engineering and research capabilities to conduct complex autonomous AI research.

The agents independently managed data processing, algorithm modification, hyperparameter tuning, and result analysis within a sandboxed environment, using known methods such as supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, weight merging, and self-distillation. This demonstration marks the first time frontier agents have autonomously post-trained a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model, suggesting that current AI agents possess the engineering and research capabilities to conduct complex autonomous AI research.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement, in which AI systems build stronger AI systems, is one promising route to superintelligence. We study a weaker form that can be measured today: frontier agents post-training a small raw base model with public data, as a test of their research potential. We build Athanor, an open agent-native system for autonomous post-training research (AutoPostTrain) on real GPUs. We give the agents full research autonomy, low-friction engineering tools, and efficient starter code. The agents carry out the research themselves: they read datasets and evaluation results, build their training data, write and modify training algorithms, tune hyperparameters, and analyze the results to decide what to try next. They work in a sandbox and cannot use external teacher models. Athanor's services supply frozen evaluation, managed jobs, decontaminated data, a persistent research record, and a held-out suite the agents are unaware of. In a 104-hour campaign, a team of four Claude Opus 5.5 agents, each on an eight-GPU node and given no research advice, improves Qwen3-4B-Base from 15.9 to 67.3 on a six-task development suite and from 9.2 to 48.2 on a held-out suite, against 66.5 and 47.9 for the official Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that a team of frontier agents can autonomously post-train a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model that matches or surpasses the official instruct version on average. The campaign's full record shows that the agents reach this level by recombining known methods and each other's models: SFT on public reasoning data, RL with a rollout change one agent introduced, weight merges across agents, and rounds of self-distillation. With execution handled, today's agents already have the engineering and research ability to conquer this task. We hope Athanor provides a foundation for scaling autonomous AI research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When humans collaborate with AI agents on long-horizon tasks, what happens to the agents' contributions? For solving long-horizon tasks, humans place greater importance on ongoing interaction with AI agents (e.g., revising plans) than on an agent's ability to complete the task in a single attempt. However, most agentic benchmarks have focused more on automation. Strong performance on such benchmarks does not imply effective real-world collaboration. Professional workflows offer a useful setting, as they often involve interdependent steps. To address this gap, we introduce Kolab, a new dataset of 115+ hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with agents on realistic, long-horizon problems. Kolab also contains participants' collaboration and output quality judgments. Our analysis reveals diverse collaboration patterns, highlighting the importance of when and how professionals coordinate with agents. A collaborative agent must do two things that automation benchmarks never test: anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject its contribution once it leaves the chat window to guide its next steps, and assess collaboration quality from the unfolding workflow without constant expert feedback. Our benchmark operationalizes both: (1) forecasting how professionals use agent contributions at diverse workflows, and (2) verifying their judgments of collaboration satisfaction and output quality. Findings show that frontier models, both agentic and non-agentic, overestimate collaboration with experts and struggle to distinguish between high- and low-quality collaboration. Longer workflow context does not consistently improve these predictions. As frontier agents cannot yet understand long-horizon collaboration with experts, we position Kolab as a valuable dataset for studying human-agent collaboration grounded in real professional workflows.

items.title: Researchers identify fundamental limits in automated self-improvement evaluation for autonomous AI agents, showing no terminating procedure can guarantee both reliability and non-conservatism in general settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Self-Improvement Problem
items.summary:
Researchers analyze the challenge of safely enabling autonomous AI agents to self-improve by proposing updates to their own components. They formalize the problem by modeling agents as programs and defining improvement via a semantic score that may be uncomputable, demonstrating that no terminating, computable gate can reliably approve only genuine improvements without missing some, due to inherent self-referential limitations.

The study distinguishes between general unbounded settings, where correctness guarantees fail, and bounded practical regimes with finite evaluation and proposal budgets, where exhaustive simulation can yield reliable search procedures. However, even in bounded settings, sequences of accepted updates can misleadingly increase bounded scores while the true semantic quality declines, highlighting intrinsic challenges in designing safe self-improving AI systems.

The study distinguishes between general unbounded settings, where correctness guarantees fail, and bounded practical regimes with finite evaluation and proposal budgets, where exhaustive simulation can yield reliable search procedures. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21646v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the rise of large language models, agentic systems are becoming increasingly autonomous, as they write code, call tools, revise prompts, and propose modifications to their own components. This autonomy raises a fundamental question for safe self-improvement: can an automated gate like a reward model or an automated reviewer reliably decide whether a proposed update should be accepted? The difficulty is structural. The gate must be a terminating, computable procedure, while the property we ultimately care about, namely whether an update is a genuine semantic improvement, depends on potentially unbounded program behavior. We formalize this mismatch by modeling agents as programs and defining improvement in terms of a semantic score that need not be computable. We study two evaluation abstractions. The first is a certifier that approves or rejects an update. The second is a search procedure that, given access to a proposal generator, attempts to output some improving candidate if one exists. We show that, in the fully general setting, no terminating procedure can simultaneously guarantee reliability (never accepting a non-improvement) and non-conservatism (never missing an available improvement): self-referential constructions can force any such gate or searcher to fail. Randomized gates with bounded error face the same limit. We then identify a standard decidable regime used in practice (bounded evaluation and a finite proposal budget) under which exhaustive simulation yields a terminating search procedure with the desired guarantees. We also show the limit of this recovery: a chain of accepted updates can raise the bounded score in every round while the true score falls. Our results draw a boundary between unbounded, universal settings where correctness guarantees collapse and bounded settings where they can be recovered by design.

items.title: DeciCAD introduces a domain-native harness for CAD agents that improves action policy learning and execution through supervised fine-tuning and geometry-grounded reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
items.summary:
DeciCAD presents a new approach for computer-aided design (CAD) agents by using a domain-specific harness that defines semantic actions, observations, and state transitions. This harness shapes the decision space for large language model agents, enabling improved policy learning and execution in the CAD domain characterized by persistent state and geometric constraints. The system uses a learning pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning and online reinforcement learning to enhance agent performance.

Evaluated across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves higher F1 scores and intersection over union (IoU) metrics while significantly reducing model output tokens compared to a general-purpose coding harness. Its supervised fine-tuning policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms coding-based policies, with reinforcement learning further increasing geometry availability and F1 to 0.7880. These results highlight the impact of the harness-defined decision space on agent behavior and policy learning in CAD tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21755v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.

items.title: Researchers develop MLExpert, a 35B parameter agentic model for autonomous machine learning engineering that improves optimization performance on MLE-Bench Lite and generalizes to other tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering
items.summary:
Researchers propose MLExpert, a 35 billion parameter Mixture-of-Experts agentic model designed for autonomous long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) optimization. The model uses a post-training method involving hierarchical supervised fine-tuning and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning to improve experiment orchestration and optimization strategies based on execution feedback. MLExpert was evaluated on MLE-Bench Lite, where it increased the average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger models like Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3.

The team developed the Kaggle-MLE Factory to create executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. MLExpert's learned optimization capabilities also improved results on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, indicating its potential to generalize across various machine learning engineering tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.22344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.

items.title: Researchers explore three diffusion-LLM parameterizations for permutation generation, evaluating their performance on Amazon recommendation reranking tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Exploring the Design Space of Permutation Diffusion LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers studied permutation generation with language models using three diffusion-LLM parameterizations: hard-assignment prediction over shuffled candidate-index sequences, soft-assignment prediction over doubly stochastic matrices, and direct ordering-score prediction followed by sorting. They evaluated these methods on recommendation reranking across three Amazon domains with candidate sets of size 10 and 20, finding that hard- and soft-assignment variants achieved Recall@1 comparable to a constrained masked-diffusion baseline, while direct ordering-score prediction guaranteed valid permutations without additional normalization steps.
The study showed that additional function evaluations did not consistently improve ranking quality and that the effectiveness depended strongly on the state representation and training objective. The results suggest that corruption, prediction parameterization, objective, and decoder should be designed jointly for permutation diffusion with language-model denoisers to optimize performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20635v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Permutation generation with language models requires both text-conditioned ranking and a global one-to-one assignment between candidates and output positions. We study this problem through three diffusion-LLM parameterizations: hard-assignment prediction over shuffled candidate-index sequences, soft-assignment prediction over doubly stochastic matrices, and direct ordering-score prediction followed by sorting. The three families place permutation constraints at different stages of prediction and decoding and therefore support different training objectives and sampling procedures. We evaluate these designs on recommendation reranking across three Amazon domains with candidate sets of size 10 and 20. At one function evaluation, the hard- and soft-assignment variants achieve Recall@1 comparable to a constrained masked-diffusion baseline, whereas direct ordering-score prediction guarantees valid permutations without Hungarian assignment or Sinkhorn normalization. Additional function evaluations do not consistently improve ranking quality, and their effect depends strongly on the state representation and training objective. These results show that corruption, prediction parameterization, objective, and decoder should be designed jointly for permutation diffusion with language-model denoisers.

items.originalTitle: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Verdict-MQ, a 395M-parameter open encoder designed to automate organizational decision-making by reading a case once and answering multiple typed questions independently. The model uses a structured attention mask to ensure question independence and option order invariance, outperforming a 421M-parameter specialist model on a typed-decisions benchmark with higher accuracy and better agreement with benchmark labels.

Verdict-MQ shows mixed results on other benchmarks like RACE, BoolQ, and MultiRC, winning on MultiRC but losing on RACE and BoolQ due to training instability. A controlled comparison reveals that providing each question with its own question-aware state copy improves accuracy on some benchmarks but increases latency by 1.4 to 2.5 times, while Verdict-MQ maintains invariance guarantees without measurable latency cost on typed decisions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20778v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.

items.title: Researchers propose CoTranslator to convert reverse chain-of-thought responses into verified forward responses for efficient reasoning distillation in AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CoTranslator: Reverse to Forward Chain-of-Thought Translator for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary:
CoTranslator is a new method designed to improve reasoning distillation by translating reverse chain-of-thought (CoT) responses, which condition on known answers, into verified forward CoT responses that do not rely on answers. This approach addresses the inefficiency and potential mismatch in existing methods by training on a small set of paired reverse and forward responses to enable large-scale generation and verification of training data for student AI models.

Evaluated across six student models on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improved average accuracy by up to 5.82 percentage points over semantic suppression methods. It retained 95.0% of the accuracy of rejection sampling while using only 35.9% of the compute for two 4-billion-parameter students. The method also transferred effectively without retraining to new datasets, different teachers, and STEM problems, boosting average STEM accuracy by 4.88 and 4.31 percentage points for 4B and 8B parameter students, respectively.

These results demonstrate that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable solution for reasoning distillation, reducing computational costs while maintaining high accuracy across diverse tasks and models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning distillation requires chain-of-thought (CoT) data with correct answers, but obtaining such data efficiently remains challenging. Forward CoT generation (FCG) followed by rejection sampling (RS) produces verified, question-only responses, yet may require many teacher calls for difficult problems. Reverse CoT generation (RCG) is cheaper because it conditions on the known answer, but access to this answer can lead to post-hoc rationalization and a mismatch with the student's answer-free inference setting. We propose CoTranslator, which learns to translate reverse CoT responses toward the distribution of verified forward responses. Trained on a small set of paired reverse and rejection-sampled forward responses, it supports large-scale generation and verification of student training data. Across six student models evaluated on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improves average accuracy over semantic suppression by up to $5.82$ percentage points. For two 4B students, it retains $95.0\%$ of rejection sampling's average accuracy while using $35.9\%$ of its estimated compute. Without retraining, the same translator transfers to a new mathematics dataset, a different teacher, and STEM problems, improving average STEM accuracy by $4.88$ and $4.31$ percentage points for 4B and 8B students, respectively. These results show that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable approach to reasoning distillation.

items.title: Researchers find majority-vote rewards in reinforcement learning track verifiable rewards due to error incoherence across prompts, preserving update direction despite label errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Wrong Votes, Right Gradients: Why Majority-Vote Rewards Track Verifiable RL
items.summary:
A new study explains why reinforcement learning using self-generated labels, such as majority votes over a model's own outputs, often achieves similar gains to training with verifiable rewards. The researchers show that at practical batch sizes, individual prompt gradients contribute minimally to output changes, so incorrect labels only affect learning if errors align coherently across prompts. They demonstrate that majority-vote updates closely match gold-standard updates when errors are incoherent, and that random label flips up to 30% do not disrupt the update direction.

The team measured per-response gradients across five models and found majority-vote errors as incoherent as random noise, with update directions agreeing as closely as independent gold updates. However, label errors following a shared pattern or reward models favoring certain responses degrade this alignment. While the equivalence between majority-vote and gold-reward updates holds locally at checkpoints, gold-reward training still outperforms on held-out accuracy. The findings highlight that error coherence, rather than error rate, determines when self-generated labels can substitute for verified rewards in reinforcement learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.20898v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with self-generated labels, such as majority vote over a model's own samples, often recovers most of the gain of training with verifiable rewards. This is puzzling from the usual prompt-level view, in which majority vote only returns a model's modal answer and cannot add information about correctness. We argue that the relevant unit is the batch-level update. Because parameters are shared, a prompt's own gradient accounts for less than 1\% of the change in that prompt's output at practical batch sizes, so a wrong label matters only to the extent that label errors share a direction across prompts. We decompose the majority-vote update into shrinkage and misdirection relative to the gold update, and show that misdirection vanishes with batch size whenever errors are incoherent across prompts, however often the labels are wrong. Measuring per-response gradients on five models, we find that majority-vote errors are as incoherent as a random-reward null, that the majority-vote update agrees with the gold update as closely as two independent gold updates agree with each other, and that its noise-corrected cosine with the gold update is 1 within error. Randomly flipping up to 30\% of gold labels leaves the update direction intact, while the same fraction flipped by a shared rule destroys it, and rewards that favor a kind of response on every prompt, such as a learned reward model, fall measurably short. The equivalence holds at every checkpoint we examine but is local: gold-reward training still ends ahead on held-out majority accuracy. Error coherence, not error rate, determines when self-generated labels can stand in for verification.

items.title: Researchers analyze unembedding matrix dynamics in language model pretraining, revealing early encoding of task information before readout expression in Pythia model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learning to Read Out: Unembedding Dynamics in Language Model Pretraining
items.summary:
Researchers studied when language models acquire capabilities by examining the unembedding matrix, or readout, during pretraining. They found that models encode task information in hidden states before the readout expresses it, causing output-based timelines to conflate encoding and expression. Using a new method called parameter-trajectory crosscoding, they identified a narrow early window in Pythia's pretraining when the readout reorganizes and word categories become decodable, while hidden states already contain task information not yet reflected in outputs.

To explore the effect of readout learning speed, the team pretrained small models with varying readout learning rates and observed that higher rates led to earlier readout development and closure of the gap between encoding and expression, without significantly affecting final loss. These findings suggest that early behavioral milestones in training may reflect when the readout learns to express information rather than when the model actually learns it.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does a language model acquire a capability? Developmental studies usually answer this by tracking when models start producing the correct token. But that prediction passes through the unembedding matrix, or readout, which is itself still being learned during pretraining. We show that a model's hidden states can encode task information before its own readout expresses it, so timelines read from outputs conflate what the model encodes with what its readout expresses. To track the readout directly, we introduce parameter-trajectory crosscoding, which fits one sparse dictionary to every token's readout row at every checkpoint. Unlike crosscoders on activations, it needs only checkpoint weights. We use it to locate a narrow early window, 0.4-1.1% of the way through Pythia's pretraining, in which the readout reorganizes and WordNet word categories become decodable from its rows. By then, linear probes on the hidden states already decode task information that the model's own outputs do not yet show. To test whether such gaps depend on how fast the readout learns, we pretrain small models from scratch that differ only in the readout's learning rate. We find that raising it makes the readout develop earlier and the gap close sooner, with little effect on final loss. Together, these results imply that early in training, where many developmental transitions are dated, a behavioral date can reflect when the readout learns to express task information and not when the model learns it.

items.title: Researchers introduce PremiseCheck, a framework combining LLM rewriting and decision models to efficiently fact-check peer review comments across NLP, machine learning, and natural sciences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PremiseCheck: Efficient Fact-Checking of Human and AI Peer Reviews
items.summary:
PremiseCheck addresses the challenge of factual errors in peer review comments, which can misstate paper content and strain the review process amid growing submissions. The framework uses a large language model (LLM) to rewrite review comments into explicit premises without reading the entire paper, then applies a decision model to verify each premise against the paper. This approach achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 at roughly half the cost and significantly reduced latency, particularly in NLP reviews.

The researchers also introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels factual errors in review comments under a unified definition across multiple scientific fields, measuring accuracy alongside cost and latency. PremiseCheck improves over existing methods by efficiently handling comments that mix several implicit assertions, combining the strengths of expensive LLM checks and cheaper decision models to optimize fact-checking performance.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.

items.title: Researchers release ToolBottleneckBench to measure tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets across 21 configurations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ToolBottleneckBench: Measuring Tool-Agent Performance under Controlled Pressures and Fixed Harness Budgets
items.summary:
ToolBottleneckBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate tool-agent performance by varying pressures such as the registered tool catalog, visible tool menu, certified workflow, and encoding of returned records while keeping synthetic enterprise tasks fixed. The benchmark uses an exact grader to identify the first unmet obligation in failed episodes and the harness limits that cause failures, revealing that the visible tool menu imposes the largest penalty on model performance, primarily due to truncation at the completion cap.

Tests across 21 model and harness configurations show that increasing the completion cap significantly reduces penalties related to truncation. Most failures occur due to harness limits, and failure records do not reliably indicate the pressure causing the failure beyond tool call counts. The study also finds that certain repairs affecting tool access or call issuance outperform configuration changes, though none improve model behavior directly. The researchers recommend reporting pressure effects alongside the harness budgets used and have made the benchmark publicly available on GitHub.
items.description:
ToolBottleneckBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate tool-agent performance by varying pressures such as the registered tool catalog, visible tool menu, certified workflow, and encoding of returned records while keeping synthetic enterprise tasks fixed. The benchmark uses an exact grader to identify the first unmet obligation in failed episodes and the harness limits that cause failures, revealing that the visible tool menu imposes the largest penalty on model performance, primarily due to truncation at the completion cap.

Tests across 21 model and harness configurations show that increasing the completion cap significantly reduces penalties related to truncation. Most failures occur due to harness limits, and failure records do not reliably indicate the pressure causing the failure beyond tool call counts. The study also finds that certain repairs affecting tool access or call issuance outperform configuration changes, though none improve model behavior directly. The researchers recommend reporting pressure effects alongside the harness budgets used and have made the benchmark publicly available on GitHub.
items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21098v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The success score of a tool agent reflects both its model and the budgets of the harness that runs it. We present ToolBottleneckBench, a benchmark that measures tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets. Synthetic enterprise tasks stay fixed while one pressure varies: the registered tool catalog, the visible tool menu, the certified workflow, or the encoding of returned records. An exact grader records the first unmet obligation of each failed episode and the harness limit, if any, that ended it. Across 21 model and harness configurations, the visible menu is the only one of the three pressures that act on the model with a large penalty, and this penalty tracks truncation at the completion cap. Raising the cap sixteenfold removes most of the penalty in the truncation-heavy configurations. Most failures end at a harness limit, and the failure record identifies the assigned pressure no more reliably than a count of tool calls. The repairs that help change which tools reach the model or who issues the calls, and only two repairs, neither improving model behavior, beat every configuration switch. We recommend reporting pressure effects with the harness budgets under which they were measured. We release the benchmark at https://github.com/zichuanxu/tool-bottleneck-bench.

items.title: Researchers find large language models share a working memory readout bottleneck due to interference rather than attention precision across multiple model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed 15 pretrained large language models (LLMs) from three families, ranging from 70 million to 14 billion parameters, and minimal transformers trained from scratch to investigate working memory limitations on the N-back task. They found that while attention mechanisms correctly locate target items, errors arise from interference caused by competing items during readout, rather than from imprecise attention focusing. Suppressing non-target item identities improved model sensitivity, especially in larger models where the task is distributed across more attention heads.

The study distinguishes between two hypotheses for LLM working memory limits: a precision account where attention fails to focus on the correct item, and an interference account where correct items are attended but corrupted by competing content. Results showed that sharpening attention had minimal effect, whereas reducing interference significantly enhanced performance, aligning with interference-based theories of human working memory. In minimal transformers, a second attention layer helped overcome precision constraints, indicating that readout interference is the primary bottleneck in LLM working memory.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21176v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

items.title: Researchers propose RaRE, a judge ensemble strategy for Rubrics as Rewards in reinforcement learning, improving performance by weighting confident judges and excluding high-disagreement cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Judging the Judges: Confidence and Disagreement in Rubrics as Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers introduce RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a method that enhances reinforcement learning in non-verifiable domains by using multiple LLM judges to score responses against structured rubrics. RaRE employs a soft-Likert reward system that weights judges based on confidence and a drop-on-disagreement mask to exclude inconsistent evaluations, addressing score variability caused by judge identity.

The study demonstrates that RaRE outperforms single-judge approaches on benchmarks like HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, leveraging the complementary strengths of different judges. This approach highlights judge ensembling as a promising direction for improving reinforcement learning with rubrics in complex evaluation settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.21179v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rubrics as Rewards (RaR) extends reinforcement learning to non-verifiable domains by using an LLM judge to score responses against a structured rubric. Prior work has focused on improving the rubric or strengthening the single judge, with comparatively little attention to how different single or multiple judges might be used during RaR training. We first show that judge identity alone produces a substantial spread in scores when training Qwen3-4B-Base on RaR-Medicine and RaR-Science across five frontier and open-weight judges. Building on this, we propose RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a novel judge ensemble strategy for RaR with two mechanisms: a soft-Likert reward that uses judge logprobs to weight more confident judges more heavily, and a drop-on-disagreement mask that excludes high-disagreement rollouts from the GRPO update. We find that this design is critical: while a naive average of judge scores fails to outperform the best single judge, RaRE outperforms every single-judge RaR variant on both HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, with per-theme analysis showing that it inherits the complementary strengths of its constituent judges. Our findings establish judge ensembling as a compelling axis for improving RaR.

items.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur, and even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction, and evaluate the resulting supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the tested prompt transformations produce a reproducible redistribution profile on these excluded variants. We then separate recurring representation change from signed readout contribution and decision failure. For a fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. RSS therefore provides a way to identify recurring sparse representation changes and quantify their contribution to a downstream readout without equating representation change with failure. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score

items.title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1?
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.

items.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) represent model activations with sparse, linearly decoded features, but the downstream effects of those features need not compose additively. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), which measure the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR is exactly the normalized energy of interactions above that order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low order approximation. To distinguish compositionality associated with the SAE representation from that induced by downstream computation, we compare learned SAE coordinates with sum preserving random rotations of the same selected subspace and find lower first order residuals for the learned coordinates across all 18 model and behavior settings. The coordinates are nevertheless not fully additive: pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in every setting and outperform parameter matched models using randomly selected third order terms. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. Together, these results show that SAE coordinates support comparatively compositional behavioral descriptions while faithful joint explanations and interventions still require interactions beyond individual feature effects. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/SAE-Behavioral-Compositionality.

items.title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $\tau^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.

items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

items.title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.

items.title: FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.

items.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.21739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.

items.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.

items.title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.

items.title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from -0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models, and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.

items.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

items.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.

items.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

items.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards
items.summary: arXiv:2610.22244v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.
